clue.text: Furious as hell, beat soundly

indicators.note: soundly hints that the two words after 'as' are to be heard rather than read

parts.note: heck is the mild exclamation people say in place of hell; a tick is one beat of a clock

explanation.surface: Someone as angry as hell hands out a thorough thrashing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beat soundly' reads as a thrashing, but 'soundly' is the homophone signal: HECK and TICK said one after the other give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym in the sense of frenzied: furious activity is frantic, feverish activity.

clue.text: Pardon from a certain judge

parts.note: ex is Latin for from or out of, as in ex works
one can mean a certain, as in 'one John Smith called'
to rate something is to judge its worth

explanation.surface: A plea for mercy granted by one particular member of the bench.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' looks like a mere joining word after the definition, but it supplies EX.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a verb: to clear someone of blame is to absolve them.

clue.text: What used to be certain when told off

indicators.note: off suggests something gone astray or spoiled, so the three words before it are disturbed

explanation.surface: Something that was once sure of itself, until it got a scolding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'told off' reads as a scolding, but 'off' alone is the anagram signal, rearranging CERTAIN WHEN TOLD.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive phrase: classical antiquity is the era that once existed and is long gone.

clue.text: Orders a suit

definitions.meaning: orders are societies or fraternities that people join, as in a religious order
one of the four suits in a pack of cards, the black trefoil one

explanation.definitionFit: Societies with members are orders, and the black trefoil cards make up one of the four suits in a pack.

clue.text: Flannel frequently found in ship by pensioner

indicators.note: found in places the word for frequently within the letters for ship

parts.note: SS is the abbreviation for steamship, crossword shorthand for a ship
oft is a poetic word for often
OAP is the British abbreviation for old age pensioner

explanation.surface: A washcloth often turns up on a boat beside a retired passenger.
explanation.walkthrough: Flannel is British for a washcloth and also slang for flattering talk, which is the sense defined; 'found in' is the insertion signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym in British slang: both mean smooth flattery meant to persuade.

clue.text: Bowler in deep after slip's vacated

indicators.note: after says the word for deep follows the emptied word
vacated empties the word of its contents, leaving only its first and last letters

parts.note: slip, with the possessive ending ignored
inner can mean deep, as in the inner meaning of a text

explanation.surface: A cricketer bowls from the outfield once the close fielder has left his post.
explanation.walkthrough: Slip and deep are cricket fielding positions, near to and far from the batsman; here 'vacated' empties SLIP to SP and 'after' orders the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Example from cricket: a slow bowler who makes the ball turn off the pitch.

clue.text: Coast resort where air's bracing?

indicators.note: bracing means clasping or holding tight, so the word for air grips the other letters

parts.note: the air of a place is its feel, its distinctive quality

indicators.note: read as re-sort, to sort again, so the letters of the word after it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A seaside town where the breeze is invigorating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resort' re-sorts WHERE into REEWH and 'bracing' has FEEL clasp it; 'Coast' is a verb here, not the seaside.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a verb: to roll along on a bicycle without pedalling.

clue.text: Process of organising teams — I say it's not difficult

indicators.note: difficult suggests awkward or troublesome, so the words before it are put out of order

explanation.surface: Sorting out the squads is easy, the speaker insists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not difficult' reads as easy, but 'difficult' alone is the anagram signal for TEAMS I SAY ITS NOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: the act of arranging things according to a method or scheme.

clue.text: Room, a dry one, and cold

parts.note: TT stands for teetotal, dry in the sense of taking no alcohol
the Roman numeral for one is I
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A chamber that is free of damp, but chilly.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the space under the roof of a house is one kind of room.

clue.text: Home studies initially in favour

parts.note: written as its initials, the institution is two letters, and those two letters sit in the middle of the word favour

explanation.surface: Learning from your own house was well regarded at first.
explanation.walkthrough: No letters are built. The British distance-learning institution is known by its initials, OU, and those letters appear inside 'favOUr'.
explanation.definitionFit: The British institution teaches degrees by distance learning, so its students work from where they live.

clue.text: Poet vaguely said "game on!"

indicators.note: said tells us to listen to the phrase, and vaguely admits the match of sounds is only rough

parts.note: tennis is a game, so 'game on' becomes 'tennis on', as when the tennis is on

explanation.surface: A versifier mumbles a challenge to begin play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vaguely said' signals an approximate homophone: 'tennis on' sounds roughly like the surname of the Victorian Poet Laureate.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Alfred, Lord of that name, was the Victorian Poet Laureate who wrote The Charge of the Light Brigade.

clue.text: From which things start to work accordingly

indicators.note: start to asks for the opening letter of the word that follows it

parts.note: hence means therefore or accordingly

explanation.surface: The source that makes everything begin operating as it should.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start to' takes the first letter of 'work'. The definition is the old relative word, as in 'from which things I conclude'.
explanation.definitionFit: Archaic relative adverb meaning from that source, or as a consequence of that.

clue.text: The second vowel has become "I"

parts.note: the vowels in order are A, E, I, O, U, so the second is E
to go is to become, as in go mad or go grey

explanation.surface: One letter of the alphabet has changed into another.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests one vowel turning into a different one; the quoted 'I' is really the self.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for I, used in psychology for the conscious self.

clue.text: Its cakes are fancy (its pies are rubbish)

definitions.note: a description of the shop rather than a synonym: the place whose cakes are elaborate

indicators.note: rubbish as an adjective means worthless or in a mess, so the three words before it are jumbled

explanation.surface: A bakery does lovely gateaux but dreadful savoury pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rubbish' is the anagram signal for ITS PIES ARE; the first four words describe the shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive: a French-style pastry shop is the place that sells elaborate gateaux and tarts.

clue.text: Narrow street to have around plaza

indicators.note: around wraps the street and possession pieces, taken together, about the word for plaza

parts.note: a mall is a shopping plaza
to own something is to have it

explanation.surface: A tight lane that will run round the square.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Narrow' wants to describe the street; it is the definition, in the sense of provincial, and 'around' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as an adjective: provincial and parochial in outlook.

clue.text: Further political sound bites

indicators.note: bites are small pieces taken out of something, so a piece of the two words before it is wanted

explanation.surface: More short quotable clips from politicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound bites' is one phrase in the surface; split it, and 'bites' says a piece is taken from 'political sound'.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as an adverb: in addition, moreover.

clue.text: Scorn about drug being put in the public eye

indicators.note: about puts the word for scorn round the word for the drug

parts.note: to slight someone is to treat them with scorn
pot is slang for cannabis

explanation.surface: Contempt over narcotics is being publicised.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a verb: to highlight something, drawing everyone's attention to it.

clue.text: Drug injected by anaemic child

indicators.note: the drug is injected by, that is taken inside, the word for anaemic

parts.note: wan means pale and sickly-looking, as an anaemic person is
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A sickly youngster gives themselves a shot of medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the Scots word for a young child, a contraction of 'wee ane', little one; 'injected by' puts E inside WAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Scots dialect noun for a youngster, from 'wee ane', little one.

clue.text: Repartee by missing husband

indicators.note: missing says the word for by lacks the letter for husband

parts.note: with can mean by, as in 'fine with me' and 'fine by me'
H is the genealogical abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: Quick banter from a spouse who has disappeared.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: clever, quick verbal humour.

clue.text: Only radio 1 gets new song

indicators.note: 1 points to the answer at 1 across, a word meaning frantic, which signals that the two words before it are thrown about

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new, as in NT for New Testament

explanation.surface: One BBC pop station alone has the latest track.
explanation.walkthrough: Radio 1 is the BBC's pop station, but '1' is a cross-reference: the answer at 1 across, HECTIC, is the anagram signal, turning ONLY RADIO into ANYOLDIRO.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a British music-hall number made famous by Harry Champion, taken from a scrap dealer's street cry.

clue.text: What might be risky to Plantagenet?

indicators.note: might be says the two words after it could become something else if rearranged

explanation.surface: Something that could endanger a medieval English king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might be' rearranges RISKY TO. The whole clue hints too: in the Wars of the Roses a white-rose supporter was a danger to the Lancastrian branch of the same royal house.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the white-rose house in the Wars of the Roses was a branch of the Plantagenet dynasty.

clue.text: One spreads cloth across top of recliner

definitions.note: one that spreads, a thing used for spreading

indicators.note: across lays the cloth over the letter, so the cloth's word spans it

parts.note: a towel is a cloth for drying

indicators.note: top of takes the first letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Someone drapes fabric over the head of an armchair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One spreads cloth' reads as a person laying fabric; 'One spreads' is a tool, 'across' puts TOWEL round R, and 'top of' picks that R.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive: a hand tool with a flat blade used to apply mortar or plaster.

clue.text: Fish — mention removing head

indicators.note: removing head strikes off the first letter of the word for mention

parts.note: to broach a subject is to mention it for the first time

explanation.surface: Talk of beheading a catch from the river.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a freshwater member of the carp family.

clue.text: Fish around lake put down, turned inside out?

indicators.note: around wraps the name of the fish about the turned-round letters

parts.note: a ray is a flat sea fish

indicators.note: turned sends the lake and put-down letters back to front as one run

parts.note: L is the map abbreviation for lake
laid is the past tense of lay, to put down

explanation.surface: A catch landed at the water's edge is set down and flipped the wrong way round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned inside out' is not one phrase: 'turned' gives DIALL, 'around' wraps the fish about it, and 'inside out' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Whimsical description: like spokes, running from the centre towards the edge.

clue.text: Thus old man's put up wall sections

indicators.note: in a down clue put up sends both pieces upwards, so the run reads from the bottom

parts.note: so means thus, in this way
old man is slang for father, dad

explanation.surface: And so father has erected some partitions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' turns SO plus DAD upside down as one run; each of these is the lower part of a room's wall, decorated differently from the upper.
explanation.definitionFit: The lower parts of interior walls, finished differently from the area above.

clue.text: Not bad, using bow to wrap imaginary cat?

indicators.note: to wrap has the bow-using word enclose the imaginary cat

parts.note: fiddling is playing the violin, which is done with a bow
air marks something mimed, as in air guitar, so here it stands for imaginary
a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: A decent attempt at tying a ribbon round a make-believe pet.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark excuses the whimsy: the imaginary cat is coined by analogy with air guitar, and 'to wrap' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom meaning moderately good, just above average.

clue.text: Detective story with half-hearted gangster element

indicators.note: the gangster's heart is a pair of the same letter, and half-hearted keeps only one of the pair

parts.note: hood is American slang for a gangster, short for hoodlum
an element is a unit, one component part of a whole

explanation.surface: A crime novel featuring a not very committed mobster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-hearted' drops one of the two Os at the heart of HOOD, leaving HOD.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a mystery novel in which the reader works out who the culprit is.

clue.text: "All shook up", not as a piece of music

indicators.note: all shook up says every one of the three words after it has been shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: The Elvis hit, though not in the form of a classical composition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All shook up' is an Elvis Presley hit in the surface, but here it is the anagram signal for NOT AS A.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a classical composition in several movements for one or two instruments.
